grades.title: Grade 9 - Foundations
goals: Build curiosity about human behavior and mental health
Start habit tracking and observation skills

psychTopics: What is psychology? Branches (clinical, cognitive, social, I-O)
projects: Behavior journal (2 weeks): triggers -> behaviors -> outcomes
Mini research: design a survey for study habits (10+ responses)
Presentation: one psychology field + one real job

skills: Digital literacy and safe online research
activities: Join or start a psychology club
Volunteer 10-20 hours (community center, tutoring, elder care)
Watch an intro series (CrashCourse Psychology) and take notes
Interview a counselor/therapist: "What do you do weekly?"
milestones: Write one 2-3 page psychology topic report
Create a one-page career map: education -> job -> employers
recommendations: Focus on observation, empathy, health science, and accurate note-taking.
Build one small behavior journal project and one presentation about a psychology career.
Practice separating facts, feelings, thoughts, and behavior in everyday examples.
applicationEvidence: Short report on one psychology topic.
nextSteps: Choose one psychology field to follow for the year.
Ask a counselor or teacher about school psychology electives.
Start a portfolio folder.

grades.title: Grade 10 - Brain & Behavior Systems
goals: Understand brain systems that impact behavior

projects: Sleep study: log 14 days -> chart outcomes

activities: Volunteer: youth mentoring or crisis-support training (age-appropriate)
Join science fair with a behavior topic
Start a basic portfolio folder (reports + reflections)
milestones: Complete a small survey study (20+ responses)
recommendations: Strengthen biology, writing, and early data interpretation.
Use sleep, stress, attention, and social influence as safe applied topics.
Begin comparing clinical, research, UX, school, and workplace psychology paths.
nextSteps: Find one community volunteer option.
Track one behavior-health question for two weeks.
Save three possible internship or summer program ideas.
studyFocus: Charts, survey results, and simple interpretation.

grades.title: Grade 11 - Research & Applied Psychology
goals: Learn research methods and ethics deeper

projects: Design an experiment (simple): hypothesis -> variables -> procedure
Literature review (5 credible sources) on one topic

activities: Volunteer at hospital/community mental health org (if permitted)
Shadow a counselor, OT, social worker, or clinic admin
Try R or Python basics (optional but powerful)
recommendations: Prioritize AP Psychology, statistics, research methods, and ethical reasoning.
Start supervised exposure through school, community, lab, hospital, or nonprofit settings where allowed.
Build a resume and portfolio around evidence, not vague interest.
nextSteps: Identify five colleges or programs.
Choose one primary career path and two backups.
Prepare questions for a psychology professional interview.
studyFocus: Correlation, causation, and limits of evidence.

grades.title: Grade 12 - College & Career Launch
goals: Finalize track (clinical, research, I-O, UX, etc.)
Build a portfolio and internship plan
Understand education requirements for each role

psychTopics: Career map: BA/BS vs MA/MS vs PhD/PsyD

milestones: Pick a primary pathway and 2 backups
Have 10 employers saved with entry roles
recommendations: Finalize a school and career launch plan with realistic education requirements.

careerPaths.title: Clinical Psychologist
careerPaths.summary: Assess, diagnose, and treat mental and emotional disorders using interviews, tests, and therapy methods.
internships: Research assistant in clinical or developmental psychology lab.
Behavioral health program assistant where permitted.
Crisis-line or peer-support training with age/scope limits.
Hospital, community, or nonprofit volunteer role focused on observation and support.
applicationPrep: Show research experience, ethical judgment, writing quality, and commitment to supervised practice.
Prepare recommendation relationships with faculty, supervisors, and research mentors.
Explain why psychology rather than general helping interest.
Track prerequisites, supervised-hour expectations, and licensure rules from official sources.
educationPath: High school: biology, statistics, writing, psychology, health science, and volunteering.
Undergraduate: psychology major or related field, research methods, statistics, lab or clinic-adjacent experience.
Graduate: PhD or PsyD for psychologist roles; supervised practicum, internship, postdoctoral hours, and licensure exam requirements vary by state.
portfolioProjects: Literature review on one disorder, treatment approach, or assessment boundary.
Ethics case analysis showing what can and cannot be concluded.
Outcome-tracking mock dashboard using fictional/de-identified data.
Reflection on shadowing, volunteering, or supervised observation.

Develop treatment plans, monitor outcomes, coordinate care, and communicate ethically with clients, families, and care teams.
Work inside strict licensure, supervision, documentation, privacy, and referral boundaries.
ethicalBoundaries: Do not diagnose, treat, or assess outside licensed/supervised authority.
Protect privacy and avoid using identifiable client stories in portfolios.
Use referral and crisis escalation pathways when safety is involved.
typicalSettings: Veterans, correctional, school, or public service settings.
studyFocus: Ethics, privacy, cultural humility, and trauma-informed care.
Developmental, cognitive, biological, and social bases of behavior.
nextSteps: Build research and volunteer evidence this term.
Study licensure requirements for the state or country of interest.
Interview a licensed psychologist about training realities.
Create a graduate-school readiness checklist.

careerPaths.summary: Study how people interact with products and systems; run studies to improve design and usability.
applicationPrep: Build two or three clean case studies that show question, method, evidence, decision, and limitation.
Practice explaining tradeoffs to non-research stakeholders.
Prepare behavioral interview stories about ambiguity, ethics, and influence.
Use company job descriptions to mirror role language.
educationPath: High school: psychology, writing, statistics, design or media projects.
Undergraduate: psychology, cognitive science, human factors, HCI, information science, or related field.
Graduate study can help for senior research, mixed methods, or specialized human factors roles but is not always required.
portfolioProjects: Usability study with research question, protocol, findings, limitations, and recommendations.
Interview synthesis project with coded themes.
Survey analysis around behavior or motivation.
Accessibility heuristic review connected to cognitive load.

Plan interviews, usability studies, surveys, diary studies, experiments, and synthesis sessions.
Turn user evidence into product recommendations without overclaiming beyond the data.

Separate user need from business pressure when reporting evidence.
studyFocus: Cognitive psychology, attention, memory, decision-making, perception, and problem-solving.
Research design, sampling, interviewing, survey design, usability methods, and statistics.
Ethics, consent, privacy, accessibility, and inclusive research.
Communication, storytelling, product thinking, and stakeholder synthesis.

Write a case study with screenshots, method, findings, and next steps.

Distinguish business preference from psychological evidence.
typicalSettings: Large employers and HR analytics teams.
studyFocus: Statistics, survey design, and people analytics.
Leadership, motivation, teams, job analysis, and organizational development.
Ethics, fairness, adverse impact, and privacy.

Statistics, experiments, research methods, and program evaluation.

Map barriers and supports.
Design a small ethical intervention plan.

coreSkills.title: Observation
coreSkills.summary: Practice noticing behavior, context, timing, emotion, environment, and changes before interpreting meaning.
coreSkills.why: Careful observation is the foundation of psychology learning because it slows down guessing and keeps evidence separate from assumptions.
uses: Record what happened, where, when, and who was present.
Separate observable behavior from interpretation or judgment.
Track what happened before and after the behavior.
Use observations to form better questions, not final conclusions.
examples: Classroom: student looked away after feedback, then stopped writing for five minutes.
Study habit: phone notifications increased during homework and breaks became longer.
Volunteer setting: participant joined more when instructions were visual and step-by-step.
Communication: tone changed after a deadline or expectation was clarified.
cardSurface: Best for: case studies, school projects, internships, and behavioral journals.
Inputs: setting, time, observed behavior, antecedent, consequence, and context.
Output: clean observation note and possible next question.
Boundary: observation does not equal diagnosis or motive-reading.
expandedCategories: Behavior: observable action, duration, frequency, intensity, and change over time.
Context: place, time, task, people present, environmental cues, and social pressure.
Before/after: antecedents, consequences, supports, barriers, and what changed.
Limits: observation cannot prove motives, diagnoses, personality, or private experience by itself.
practicePrompts: Write the note without using labels or motive words.
What happened before the behavior, and what happened after?
What would I need to observe again before calling this a pattern?

Use respectful language that preserves dignity and choice.

Interview: describe helping experience without exposing private stories.

Professional growth: documentation, supervision, reflective practice, and respectful interview stories.

coreSkills.title: Ethical Reasoning
coreSkills.summary: Check privacy, consent, scope, safety, supervision, equity, respectful language, and possible unintended consequences.
coreSkills.why: Every psychology activity should consider who could be helped, harmed, exposed, pressured, mislabeled, or misunderstood.
uses: Identify the people affected and the information involved.
Check consent, privacy, vulnerability, power differences, and supervision.
Consider harms, benefits, alternatives, and what should not be done.
Write the safest educational next step and the right escalation path.
examples: Do not ask classmates to reveal trauma, diagnoses, or private family information for a casual project.
Do not call a case subject depressed, anxious, or disordered without qualified assessment.
Do not use company or internship data in a portfolio unless approved and de-identified.
Do ask for supervision when a situation involves safety, mandated reporting, or clinical concerns.

Good offers are narrow, ethical, measurable, and referral-aware.

cards.title: Business Models
cards.summary: Compare service, coaching, school program, research support, analytics, dashboard, content, and software models for applied cognitive work.
cards.whyThisMatters: A business model makes the user clarify who is served, what is delivered, how quality is protected, and how outcomes are reviewed.
useThisInPractice: Choose one delivery model before designing features or services.
Define pricing, support, quality review, privacy boundaries, and referral rules.
Tie the model to a career path, tool workflow, and portfolio project.
details: Possible models include workshops, school programs, research support, survey analysis, portfolio coaching, behavior-change education, and software dashboards.
Each model needs privacy, consent, quality review, and referral boundaries.
recommendedActions: Create an ethics and privacy checklist.

cards.title: Certifications
cards.summary: Track credentials, certificates, coursework, supervised requirements, and scope boundaries that support psychology-adjacent readiness.
cards.whyThisMatters: Credentials can strengthen readiness, but they must not be confused with licensure, diagnosis authority, or clinical scope.
useThisInPractice: Record each certification with issuer, date, renewal, and role relevance.
Separate certificates from licenses and supervised clinical authority.
Connect every credential to a portfolio project or internship requirement.
details: Certificates can support readiness but are not the same as licensure.
Track issuer, expiration, renewal, scope, and role relevance.
recommendedActions: Separate certificate, degree, license, and supervised experience.

cards.title: Portfolio Projects
cards.summary: Build evidence through survey studies, usability studies, behavior-change plans, literature reviews, dashboards, and ethics-aware case analyses.
cards.whyThisMatters: Projects make skills inspectable and help schools, employers, and collaborators understand what the learner can actually do.
useThisInPractice: Keep each project tied to a career path and a Core concept.
Include question, method, ethics note, result, limitation, and next action.
Use report export to turn saved work into a professional summary.
details: Strong projects include survey studies, literature reviews, usability studies, behavior-change plans, case analyses, dashboards, and ethics reviews.
Every project should show question, method, evidence, limitation, and next step.
recommendedActions: Add an ethics note to each.
Tie each project to a career path.

cards.title: School Roadmap
cards.summary: Connect grade-level and post-secondary learning to psychology topics, projects, milestones, internships, and career paths.
cards.whyThisMatters: A school roadmap helps the learner choose classes, projects, activities, and application evidence in the right order.
useThisInPractice: Review the current grade or school stage.
Pick one project and one activity for the current term.
Map courses and milestones to a career path before applying.
details: Grade-level planning should connect classes, psychology topics, activities, projects, milestones, and applications.
Post-secondary planning should compare undergraduate, graduate, licensure, research, and applied industry paths.
recommendedActions: Pick one project and one application milestone.

cards.title: Skills Builder
cards.summary: Develop research design, statistics, ethics, communication, empathy, data tools, survey design, dashboards, and applied analysis skills.
cards.whyThisMatters: Skills become useful when they are practiced through projects and connected to real career or school evidence.
useThisInPractice: Choose one core skill and one tool skill.
Practice the skill through a small project.
Save the evidence to a portfolio or report.
details: Core psychology skills include observation, ethics, communication, research design, statistics, case reasoning, survey design, and reflective practice.
Tool skills should support psychology work, not become the purpose of the app.
recommendedActions: Pick one concept skill and one evidence skill.

cards.title: Application Prep
cards.summary: Prepare resumes, personal statements, cover notes, portfolios, interview answers, school applications, internships, and job applications.
cards.whyThisMatters: Application prep turns learning into a clear story with evidence, fit, boundaries, and next steps.
useThisInPractice: Create one resume or application version per role or program.
Use the opportunity description to select proof points.
Track submissions, follow-ups, interviews, and outcomes.
details: Application prep includes role research, resume, cover note, personal statement, interview stories, portfolio evidence, references, and follow-up tracking.
Each application should show fit, boundaries, and evidence.
recommendedActions: Choose a target role or program.
Track submission, follow-up, interview, and result.

cards.title: Daily Coach
cards.summary: Turns daily reflection and Core intelligence into psychology-centered recommendations across concepts, cases, tools, ethics, careers, learning actions, emotion, behavior, stress, attention, communication, and habits.
cards.whyThisMatters: Daily Coach is the single AI recommendation entry point, keeping psychology and behavioral health guidance focused, educational, and grounded in Core-owned content.
prompts: What psychology concept should I study next?
What did I notice today in emotion, behavior, stress, attention, or communication?
What evidence do I have, and what evidence is missing?
What Core tool should I use next?
What ethical boundary should I remember?
What is one safe next learning action?
outputGoal: A relevant Core tool or detail screen.
A safe report-ready note when useful.
guardrails: Education only; not diagnosis or treatment.
Do not diagnose yourself or others from a daily note.
Escalate safety concerns to appropriate trusted, school, emergency, or professional support.

cards.title: Reports
cards.summary: Prepares learning, case, career, and tool activity for professional summaries with evidence, limits, and recommendations.
cards.whyThisMatters: Reports turn learning into something the user can review, share, or use for school and career planning.
prompts: What evidence or limitation should be included?
guardrails: Reports should not claim clinical conclusions.
Keep personal or sensitive details private.

cards.title: Quiz
cards.summary: Builds review around psychology concepts, branches, behavior approaches, ethics, bias, and career readiness.
cards.whyThisMatters: Quizzes help the learner find weak spots and choose what to study next.
guardrails: Quiz results are learning signals, not professional judgments.

cards.title: Trivia
cards.summary: Uses low-pressure psychology facts to build familiarity with behavior, cognition, development, social influence, and ethics.
cards.whyThisMatters: Small facts make the domain easier to explore before deeper study.
prompts: What branch does this connect to?
guardrails: Trivia is introductory and should not replace deeper study.

cards.title: Decisions
cards.summary: Reviews psychology-related decisions for bias, evidence, uncertainty, values, consequences, and reversibility.
cards.whyThisMatters: Decision quality is a core behavioral science skill.
guardrails: Do not use this as medical, legal, or crisis advice.

cards.title: Case Studies
cards.summary: Helps analyze educational cases through observation, behavior, possible explanations, evidence, ethics, and boundaries.
cards.whyThisMatters: Case work trains careful reasoning without jumping to diagnosis.
guardrails: Educational cases are not clinical assessment.
Avoid labeling real people from limited information.

cards.title: School Roadmap
cards.summary: Connects grade level, courses, projects, study topics, applications, and milestones to psychology and behavioral health careers.
cards.whyThisMatters: A roadmap makes study choices practical and career-aware.
prompts: What grade or school stage am I in?
What should I study this term?
guardrails: Verify school and program requirements from official sources.

cards.title: Career Paths
cards.summary: Connects branches of psychology to clinical, counseling, school, research, UX, organizational, behavioral science, and public health roles.
cards.whyThisMatters: Career planning works better when roles are tied to education, evidence, ethics, and employer types.
guardrails: Licensure and clinical authority vary by location.

cards.title: Psychology Tools
cards.summary: Uses bias checks, case analysis, learning plans, surveys, ethics reviews, and scenario practice to support psychology learning.
cards.whyThisMatters: Tools should support behavioral health understanding, not become programming utilities.
prompts: What problem am I trying to understand?
outputGoal: A saved report or portfolio item.
guardrails: Tools are for education, reflection, and planning, not diagnosis.

cards.title: Companies
cards.summary: Helps identify healthcare, research, school, government, UX, technology, and community organizations to investigate or apply to.
cards.whyThisMatters: Company research turns interest into real opportunities and role requirements.
prompts: What role title should I search?
What proof do I need before applying?
guardrails: Use official career pages and current employer requirements.

cards.title: Search
cards.summary: Searches Core psychology content across branches, approaches, tools, careers, companies, school roadmap, cases, and resources.
cards.whyThisMatters: Search helps the learner find the right Core-owned psychology content quickly.
prompts: What topic am I looking for?
Is it a branch, approach, tool, career, or company?
guardrails: Search returns learning content; verify external requirements from official sources.
